tldr: For long-horizon whole-body loco-manipulation tasks where a humanoid robot sequentially transports multiple large objects without environment resets, this paper proposes "Humanoid Horizon"—a single unified policy framework combining parallel training, a dynamic starting mechanism, and reward gating. It achieves over 80% success rates on each stage of a two-object sequential transport benchmark, while showing high robustness when scaling to five objects and when distilled into a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) student model driven by egocentric vision and language instructions.
hero_caption: A humanoid robot sequentially transporting multiple objects without environment resets across cluttered environments such as bedrooms, kitchens, living rooms, and warehouses. Each row represents a single episode, completing navigation, grasping, lifting, carrying, and placing within a single policy.
overview:
Having a humanoid robot tidy up multiple large objects sequentially without resets in cluttered indoor environments is a major challenge in robotics. Unlike wheeled bases or quadrupeds, bipedal humanoids have lower dynamic stability and must continuously maintain walking balance while using their entire body to transport items. Prior reinforcement learning approaches suffered from "easy-reward bias"—where training overemphasizes early transport stages at the expense of exploring later ones—and "catastrophic forgetting"—where learning later stages causes the policy to forget how to execute earlier ones.

To tackle this, the authors developed "Humanoid Horizon," a framework that trains the entire process using a single neural network policy. It is built on three core mechanisms. First, "Parallel Training" trains multiple transport stages concurrently across parallel streams, ensuring continuous gradient updates for all stages. Second, the "Dynamic Starting Mechanism" saves upstream terminal robot states into buffers to serve as initial states for subsequent stages, adapting the policy to distribution shifts at stage transitions. Third, "Reward Gating" zeroes out all remaining episode rewards if an immediately preceding placed object is displaced or knocked over during downstream execution, thereby preserving earlier placements.

The framework was evaluated on the LHM-Humanoid benchmark across 350 diverse indoor scenes and 66 held-out scenes. In two-object sequential transport, it achieved an overall success rate of 80.4%, significantly outperforming the previous state-of-the-art (71.1%). Furthermore, performance degraded gracefully even when extending the task to five sequential objects. Using DAgger, the policy was successfully distilled into a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model operating solely on egocentric RGB/depth observations and natural language instructions.
contributions: Proposed Humanoid Horizon, a unified policy framework that enables long-horizon multi-object sequential transport with a single whole-body control policy, without relying on external modules or environment resets.
Introduced a parallel training strategy optimizing all transport stages concurrently, mitigating easy-reward bias and catastrophic forgetting that arise in sequential curriculum learning.

Introduced a dynamic starting mechanism that cycles upstream terminal states into downstream initial states, along with reward gating that cuts off rewards upon displacement of the immediately preceding object, balancing boundary robustness and placement persistence.

Demonstrated state-of-the-art performance across 350 training scenes and 66 held-out scenes, scalability to 5-object long-horizon tasks, and successful distillation into a VLA model driven by egocentric RGB/depth and natural language instructions.

sections.heading: Why is it so hard for humanoids to tidy up multiple objects sequentially?
sections.summary: In whole-body loco-manipulation for humanoid robots, executing long-horizon tasks while maintaining dynamic stability is a major challenge. When extending existing methods to sequential multi-object transport, easy-reward bias (early stages dominating optimization) and catastrophic forgetting (learning later stages while forgetting earlier ones) become critical bottlenecks. Humanoid Horizon breaks through these hurdles with a single policy combining parallel training, dynamic starting, and reward gating.
sections.details:
Whole-body loco-manipulation by humanoid robots—coordinating whole-body walking and manipulation—is one of robotics' key frontiers. Compared to standalone arms or quadrupeds, bipedal humanoids are more prone to falling and must constantly maintain balance across an entire long-horizon task chain.

However, most prior studies have been limited to short-horizon tasks transporting a single object from fixed initial states. Extending these directly to sequential multi-object transport encounters two severe issues:

- **Easy-reward bias**: Training overemphasizes early transport stages, leaving later stages insufficiently explored.
- **Catastrophic forgetting**: After mastering the first object, training on the second object starting from terminal states leads to losing the ability to transport and place the first object.

Because this forgetting occurred even in prior work like LHM-Humanoid, that approach relied on a complex pipeline training separate teacher models for each stage and distilling them later. This fails to scale as the number of objects grows.

Therefore, Humanoid Horizon takes an approach that relies entirely on a single policy $\pi_{\theta}$ without task-specific auxiliary modules or environment resets. By optimizing all stages simultaneously in parallel and naturally handing off boundary states between stages, it achieves robust control that avoids catastrophic performance degradation even as object counts increase.

sections.heading: The current landscape of physics-based motion generation and long-horizon loco-manipulation
sections.summary: Research on motion generation and environmental interaction has advanced, but much of it remains confined to short-horizon tasks using robot arms or simple mobile bases. Even in the few long-horizon loco-manipulation studies on humanoids, catastrophic forgetting and bias caused by hierarchical control or sequential training remain unsolved. This paper uniquely addresses these problems using a single policy paired with a novel state-recycling and reward design.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Physics-Based Motion Generation and Human-Environment Interaction
Motion generation in graphics and robotics has achieved dynamics-aware control through physics-based reinforcement learning, exemplified by AMP (Adversarial Motion Priors) and DeepMimic. Recent works such as InterScene and InterPhys interact dynamically with objects in the environment, and HumanVLA handles heavy objects. However, most remain limited to short-horizon tasks with single objects and fixed initial poses. While LHM-Humanoid ventured into sequential multi-object transport, it depended on sequential training and per-task custom designs, limiting its long-horizon scalability.

### 2.2 Long-Horizon Loco-Manipulation
Executing long-horizon tasks has been widely studied on stationary manipulators and mobile robots (wheeled bases with manipulators). Dominant paradigms include sub-goal decomposition, world-state prediction, and trajectory forecasting, yet these often rely on task-specific priors. On humanoids, even teleoperation is largely short-horizon and open-loop. Due to challenging state estimation, autonomous long-horizon whole-body control has seen very few attempts, such as LessMimic and LHM-Humanoid.

Furthermore, while reverse curriculum learning and reset-free reinforcement learning exist for learning inter-stage transitions, the former requires manual resets near goals, and the latter demands additional reset policies. Humanoid Horizon's dynamic starting mechanism fundamentally differs by directly feeding upstream terminal states downstream without manual resets or auxiliary policies.

sections.heading: A three-part pipeline to forge a single unified policy
sections.summary: The task requires sequentially placing multiple large objects in cluttered indoor scenes without resets. The pipeline consists of three pillars: "Parallel Training" that simultaneously updates all stages with a single policy; a "Dynamic Starting Mechanism" that overwrites and recycles upstream terminal states into downstream starting buffers; and "Reward Gating" that zeroes out subsequent rewards if the just-placed object is disturbed. Finally, the RL teacher policy is distilled into a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Task Formulation
In scene $n$, the robot sequentially transports an ordered set of objects $\{o_{1}^{n}, o_{2}^{n}, \ldots, o_{S_{n}}^{n}\}$ from initial positions to target locations. For each object, it executes four phases: (1) approaching, (2) grasping and lifting, (3) carrying, and (4) placing at the goal. Once an object is placed, the robot immediately transitions to the next object without environment resets, requiring it to turn and re-approach while navigating obstacles and recovering from post-placement pose disturbances.

### 3.2 Parallel Training Strategy
Rather than training stages sequentially, the environment pool is divided equally into $S$ stage streams, updating the shared policy parameters $\theta$ simultaneously with gradients from all streams. Stream $i$ initializes from buffer $\mathcal{B}_i$. Because gradients continuously flow from every stage, early-stage bias (easy-reward bias) and forgetting of previous stages (catastrophic forgetting) are fundamentally prevented.

### 3.3 Dynamic Starting Mechanism
At the end of each epoch, the terminal state $s_{T}^{(i,n)}$ of stage $i$ in scene $n$ is extracted to directly overwrite the downstream stage buffer $\mathcal{B}_{i+1}^{n}$. In the next epoch, stage $i+1$ initializes from this buffer.
Although each environment holds only one state, terminal states accumulate and update temporally across epochs. As upstream stages improve, downstream initial states automatically evolve into a more diverse, natural distribution, creating highly robust stage boundaries without manual curriculum design.

### 3.4 Reward Gating for Physical Plausibility
After placing the previous object $o_{i-1}^{n}$, if the robot collides with and displaces it on the way to the next object, the overall task fails. Thus, in stage $i$ ($i>1$) streams, the position of the immediately preceding object $o_{i-1}^{n}$ is continuously monitored. If its displacement from the target exceeds a threshold $\epsilon$, rewards for all remaining steps in that episode are immediately set to zero.
Because all stages share a single policy, learning this local rule—"do not disturb the immediately preceding object"—recursively gives rise to behaviors that preserve all previously placed objects.

### 3.5 Extension: Distillation into a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Policy
The RL teacher policy trained with privileged state information is distilled via DAgger into a VLA student model that relies only on egocentric cameras (RGB or depth) and natural language instructions. In this setup, users interactively provide the next instruction (e.g., "carry the laptop to the desk") after each transport stage completes.

captions.F2: Overall pipeline of Humanoid Horizon: (A) Parallel Training simultaneously optimizing S stages with a shared unified policy, (B) Dynamic Starting Mechanism overwriting downstream buffers with upstream terminal states to broaden initial state diversity, (C) Reward Gating zeroing out rewards upon displacement of the preceding object, and (D) Distillation via DAgger into a student model driven by egocentric vision and natural language instructions.

sections.heading: Validation on 350 scenes, generalization to unseen environments, and scaling to 5 objects
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted across 350 indoor scenes (bedrooms, living rooms, kitchens, warehouses) and 66 held-out scenes. On two-object sequential transport, the proposed method achieved an overall success rate of 80.4%, clearly outperforming the strongest baseline, LHM-Humanoid (71.1%). Furthermore, in an ultra-long-horizon 5-object task where baselines collapsed, it exhibited graceful degradation, and maintained strong performance when distilled into VLA models.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Dataset and Evaluation Metrics
A total of 350 cluttered layouts were used across four categories: bedrooms, living rooms, kitchens, and warehouses. Evaluation metrics include per-stage success rates (Succ1, Succ2), overall success rate completing both stages (SuccAll), and distance errors to the targets (Dist1, Dist2). A transport is judged successful if the object rests within 0.2 m of the target.

### 4.2 Main Results across 350 Tasks
- **End-to-End RL**: Sparse rewards failed to propagate through the contact-rich long-horizon task, collapsing completely with a SuccAll of 0.0%.
- **Curriculum RL**: Achieved a high Succ1 of 88.3% on the first stage, but could not master inter-stage transition motions, dropping SuccAll to 47.2% and exhibiting severe easy-reward bias.
- **Hierarchical RL / TokenHSI / InterMimic / HumanVLA**: Due to error accumulation across primitives and catastrophic forgetting, SuccAll remained between 7.5% and 29.9%.
- **LHM-Humanoid**: The strongest baseline from prior work, reaching Succ1/Succ2/SuccAll of 87.4%/72.6%/71.1%.
- **Humanoid Horizon (Ours)**: Reached 96.6%/81.3%/80.4%, surpassing the prior state of the art by about 9%. Removing dynamic starting dropped SuccAll to 67.7%, and removing reward gating dropped it to 69.6%, validating both mechanisms.

### 4.3 Generalization to 66 Unseen Tasks
On out-of-distribution novel layouts and objects, the proposed method maintained 97.1%/79.3%/78.0%. It outperformed LHM-Humanoid's SuccAll (61.6%) by roughly 16%, showing robust generalizability rather than overfitting.

### 4.4 VLA Distillation Results
In experiments distilling the RL teacher into egocentric VLA student models via DAgger, scores dropped across all methods due to the loss of privileged state inputs. However, students distilled from the proposed teacher decisively outperformed baseline student models in both RGB and depth modalities.

### 4.5 Scaling to 5 Sequential Objects
Testing extended to a demanding 5-object sequential transport setup without resets. While End-to-End RL (1.5%) and Curriculum RL (3.2%) failed completely, and even LHM-Humanoid (using five separate teacher models) sharply declined to 20.9% by stage 5, the proposed method sustained 82.2% at stage 3 and 66.5% at stage 5, demonstrating remarkable resilience with an overall SuccAll of 60.2%.

sections.heading: Failure analysis: Where does the robot stumble?
sections.summary: Humanoid Horizon exhibits two primary failure modes. The first is a performance drop from the initial stage to the second stage, stemming from the difficulty of turning and re-approaching around obstacles from an awkward post-placement pose. The second is "frozen action," where the robot reaches the object but halts without initiating a stable grasp, likely caused by uniform computational allocation across scenes of varying difficulty during training.
sections.details:
A detailed analysis of experimental results revealed two primary failure patterns in this approach:

- **Success Rate Gap between Stage 1 and Stage 2**: The drop from stage 1 (Succ1: 96.6%) to stage 2 (Succ2: 81.3%) is larger than drops between subsequent stages. This is rooted in the task structure: stage 1 begins from a clean, upright stance on open floor, whereas stage 2 begins from a perturbed pose surrounded by obstacles after completing the first placement. Obstacle-avoiding path planning to turn around and re-approach the next object is substantially more difficult.
- **Frozen Action Prior to Grasping**: In some instances, the robot reaches the target object but freezes in place without completing a stable grasp. A contributing factor is that training allocates computational resources uniformly across all scenes. Scenes with complex furniture layouts and difficult grasps require more exploration, but uniform allocation leaves them insufficiently optimized.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook: The path toward physical deployment
sections.summary: By unifying parallel training, dynamic starting, and reward gating, Humanoid Horizon achieves state-of-the-art results in long-horizon humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation. Future work focuses on overcoming current weaknesses through advanced path planning and difficulty-adaptive sampling, bridging the gap from simulation to physical humanoid deployment.
sections.details:
This paper presented "Humanoid Horizon," learning long-horizon multi-object sequential loco-manipulation on humanoids using a single policy without external modules or environment resets.

Through the synergy of three mechanisms—parallel training providing sustained gradients across all stages, dynamic starting teaching realistic inter-stage handoffs, and reward gating strictly preserving past placements—the framework broke previous limitations. It demonstrated robustness on 2-object benchmarks, 5-object long-horizon tasks, unseen environments, and distillation into vision- and language-driven VLA models.

Identified future directions include improving path planning during the transition to stage 2, introducing curriculum mechanisms that prioritize difficult scenes during exploration, and deploying the simulation-trained policy onto physical humanoid robot platforms.

sections.heading: Appendix: Robot joint configuration and training reproducibility
sections.summary: Details on the humanoid control interface, network architectures, and multi-seed training reproducibility are reported. The humanoid has 28 degrees of freedom controlled at 30 Hz. Experiments across three independent seeds showed a final success rate standard deviation below 0.3%, confirming the stability of the method.
sections.details:
### A.1–A.3 Robot Configuration and Control Interface
The humanoid model consists of 15 rigid links—including the pelvis, torso, head, arms, and legs—with a total of 28 controllable degrees of freedom (DoF). The network outputs normalized joint targets $\mathbf{a} \in [-1, 1]^{28}$, which are converted via affine transformations and sent to PD controllers. The simulation runs at 60 Hz with a control frequency of 30 Hz.
The RL teacher policy receives privileged observations (250 dimensions total + 128-dimensional BPS features), including body proprioception (225 dimensions), object pose information, navigation targets, and Basis Point Set (BPS, 200 points) features encoding object point clouds.

### Appendix B Multi-Seed Training Curve Stability
To verify robustness against stochastic factors, training was conducted across three independent seeds (seeds 0, 1, 2) for 16,000 epochs each. After rapidly adapting from the pretrained model to the parallel multi-object environment within the first 2,000 epochs, all seeds converged smoothly to an 87–89% training success rate. The standard deviation across seeds was under 0.3%, confirming that the framework's optimization is remarkably stable and insensitive to initializations.

captions.F3: Training success rate progression across 16,000 epochs for three independent random seeds. All seeds follow nearly identical trajectories and converge around 87–89%, showing that the proposed training is highly robust to initialization randomness and strongly reproducible.

takeaways: When solving long-horizon task chains via reinforcement learning, organizing all stages into parallel streams under a single shared policy prevents bias and forgetting far better than training separate per-stage policies or using sequential curriculums.

The dynamic starting mechanism, which overwrites downstream initial buffers with upstream terminal states, provides an elegant solution to bridge inter-stage distribution shifts without requiring manual reset designs.

In multi-object placement tasks, simply zeroing out episode rewards when an immediately preceding placement is disturbed naturally induces self-organized behaviors that recursively protect all past placements.

Even when an RL policy is trained with privileged state information, it can be distilled via DAgger into a VLA model driven purely by egocentric vision and language instructions while retaining high performance.
limitations: Compared to stage 1 starting from a clean initial pose, success rates still drop when transitioning into stage 2 starting from disturbed poses in cluttered spaces, posing challenges for obstacle-avoiding navigation.
Cases of "frozen action" occur where the robot reaches an object but halts without grasping, indicating the need for difficulty-adaptive sampling on challenging furniture layouts.

Evaluations in this paper remain confined to simulation environments (Isaac Gym, etc.); addressing contact-rich transport and the sim-to-real gap on physical humanoid hardware is left for future work.
